1834.t: Traditionally derived from Proto-Indo-European *skend- (“to jump”), and compared with Latin scandō (“to ascend”), Sanskrit स्कन्दति (skandati, “to jump, hop, hurry”).

1828.t: From earlier ξένϝος (xénwos), from Proto-Hellenic *ksénwos, which Beekes tentatively considers Pre-Greek; he also mentions attempts to connect the term to Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (“guest”).

1813.t: From Proto-Hellenic *gʷápt͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *gʷh₂bʰ-yé-ti, from *gʷeh₂bʰ- (“to dive, dive in”).

1880.t: Zero-grade of the root of βένθος (bénthos), of uncertain origin. Alternatively from earlier *βαφύς (*baphús), related to Sanskrit गभीर (gabhīrá, “deep”).

1846.t: From ἀ- (a-, “not”), the root of γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “know”) + -έω (-éō, verb-forming suffix). Compare ἀγνώς (agnṓs, “unknown”), ἄγνοια (ágnoia, “ignorance”).

1856.t: From ἀ- (a-, “not”) + γιγνώσκω (gignṓskō, “know”) + -ια (-iā, abstract noun suffix).

1844.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʰorós, likely from a Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰoros, from a root *ǵʰer-, though the semantic identity of this root has been disputed: * From *ǵʰer- (“to seize, catch, enclose”), with some original meaning of "encircling/ring (dance)",…

1866.t: From ἐπι- (epi-) + -φανής (-phanḗs); compare ἐπιφαίνω (epiphaínō, “to come into view”).

1881.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ǵews-. Cognates include Old English ċēosan (English choose), Latin gustō,, Sanskrit जुषते (juṣate).

1835.t: From στείχω (steíkhō, “walk, march, go or come, march in line or order”), from Proto-Indo-European *steygʰ- (“to walk”). Cognate with German steigen, English sty, stair, stile and possibly Latin vestīgō.

1814.t: From Proto-Hellenic *géronts, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵérh₂onts (“old”). Cognates include Sanskrit जर॑त् (járat, “old man”), Old Armenian ծերուն (cerun), and Middle Irish gérat (“champion”).

1896.t: From Proto-Indo-European *neyk-. Cognates include Lithuanian niekoti, Latvian niekāt, and Welsh nithio.

1886.t: Related to ζώννυμι (zṓnnūmi, “to gird”); ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *yoh₃snéh₂, from the root *yeh₃s- (“gird”). Compare Old Church Slavonic (по)ꙗсъ ((po)jasŭ), Sanskrit रास्ना (rā́snā) (< *yā́snā).

1830.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *pleth₂-? Proto-Indo-European *pel-? Proto-Indo-European *pleh₂-der. Ancient Greek πλάγος (plágos) Proto-Indo-European *-yósder.

1839.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *teḱ-der. Proto-Indo-European *títḱeti Proto-Hellenic *tíktō Ancient Greek τίκτω (tíktō) ▲ Hebrew תוךsl.

1821.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱowilos, from *ḱewH- (“hollow”) (which may be identical to *ḱewh₁- (“to swell”)).

1808.t: From Proto-Indo-European *uh₁r-. Cognates include Latin ūrīnor, Old Armenian գայռ (gayṙ), and Sanskrit वार् (vā́r), वारि (vā́ri).

1867.t: PIE word *swé From a t-extension of Proto-Indo-European *swé (“self”). Related to ἔτης (étēs, “clansman”).

1818.t: From Proto-Indo-European *yeh₃s- + -νυμι (-nūmi), related to Lithuanian júosta (“girdle”), Latvian jôsta (“girdle”), Avestan 𐬫𐬁𐬵- (yāh-, “girdle”), 𐬫𐬁𐬯𐬙𐬀 (yāsta, “girdled”), Albanian gjesh (“to gird”). See also ζώνη (zṓnē).

1847.t: From ἀνάγκη (anánkē, “force, necessity”) + -άζω (-ázō, denominative verbal suffix).

1855.t: Traditionally derived from ἀστήρ (ăstḗr, “star”) + the root *ὀπ- (*op-) underlying ὀπή (opḗ, “sight, hole”) and ὄμμα (ómmă, “eye”), thus “star-eye”; compare Old Armenian փայլակն (pʻaylakn, “lightning”) for a semantically-similar and partially-cognate (in…

1885.t: From εὐ- (eu-, “well”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”). Euphemistically refers to "left" because bad omens came from the left side.

1806.t: From the Greek descendant of Proto-Indo-European *h₃elh₁- (“destroy”) + -νυμι (-nūmĭ), with assimilation of *-λν- (*-ln-) to -λλ- (-ll-). Compare Latin ab-oleō, which may be related.

1849.t: From ἀνα- (ana-) + an unattested *ἁλίσκω (*halískō), originally meaning "to tear up"; see ἁλίσκομαι (halískomai, “to be captured”) for more on the second component.

1895.t: Of unknown origin; Beekes notes that the full grade of the stem and barytonesis of the word suggest that it was originally a noun and not an adjective, though he leaves the origin open without mentioning any potential comparanda.

1842.t: Contraction of χειμάρροος (kheimárrhoos), from χεῖμα (kheîma, “winter”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

1857.t: According to Beekes, from Pre-Greek and related to ἄχωρ (ákhōr, “scurf”) (particularly, identical to the form ἄχορα (ákhora)) and to ἄχνη (ákhnē, “foam, froth”).

1899.t: From λύω (lúō, “to set free, release”) + -τρον (-tron, “a suffix forming instrument nouns”).

1823.t: From κύμβη (kúmbē, “hollow of a vessel”), with a suffix -αλον which is found also in κρόταλον (krótalon, “rattle”).

1884.t: From δια- (dĭă-, “across, through”) + μένω (ménō, “to stay, to remain”). Related to and synonymous with Latin permaneō.

1872.t: Onomatopoeic reduplicated formation, with the same ending of ἰύζω (iúzō, “to shout, yell”).

1875.t: ὑπερ- (huper-, “above”) + ἀσπιστής (aspistḗs, “one armed with a shield”)

1878.t: From Biblical Hebrew בֵּלְטְשַׁאצַּר (Bēlṭəšaṣṣar), from Akkadian Bēl-šarra-uṣur (literally “may Baal protect the king”).

1876.t: From ὑπο- (hupo-, “hypo-, sub-”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”). Exact cognate with Latin sufferō (“to carry under, suffer”).
